section.title: The Parables of the Kingdom
section.sectionRationale: The third discourse is a string of kingdom parables. In the wake of mounting rejection, Jesus teaches in parables that both reveal and conceal, unveiling how the kingdom of heaven actually comes: sown in a word that meets varied hearts, growing secretly and small at first, mixed with evil until the harvest, worth more than everything, and ending in a final separation.
section.thesis: Through the parables Jesus discloses the mysteries of the kingdom: it comes now in a hidden, contested, growing form rather than in immediate glory, it demands a hearing heart that bears fruit, it is worth selling everything to gain, and it will be consummated at the end of the age in the gathering of the righteous and the judgment of the wicked.
section.frameNote: Seven beats: the parable of the sower; the purpose of parables; the sower explained; the wheat and the weeds; the mustard seed and leaven; the weeds explained and the end of the age; and the treasure, pearl, and net, closing with the trained scribe.

verses.text: That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea.
Such large crowds gathered around Him that He got into a boat and sat down, while all the people stood on the shore.
And He told them many things in {{parabole|parables}}, saying, “A farmer went out to sow his seed.
And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow.
But when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root.
Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings.
Still other seed fell on good soil and produced a crop, a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold.
He who has ears, let him hear.”
Then the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Why do You speak to the people in parables?”
He replied, “The knowledge of the {{mysterion|mysteries}} of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you, but not to them.
Whoever has will be given more, and he will have an abundance. Whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.
This is why I speak to them in parables: ‘Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.’
In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: ‘You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.

For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’
But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.
For truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.
Consider, then, the parable of the sower:
When anyone hears the message of the kingdom but does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. This is the seed sown along the path.
The seed sown on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy.
But since he has no root, he remains for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away.
The seed sown among the thorns is the one who hears the word, but the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.
But the seed sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and produces a crop, a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold.”

units.label: The wheat and the weeds
units.note: let both grow until the harvest

verses.text: Jesus put before them another parable: “The {{basileia|kingdom}} of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field.
But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away.
When the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the weeds also appeared.
The owner’s servants came to him and said, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?’
‘An enemy did this,’ he replied. So the servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and pull them up?’
‘No,’ he said, ‘if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them.
Let both grow together until the harvest. At that time I will tell the harvesters: First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn.’”
He put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man took and planted in his field.
Although it is the smallest of all seeds, yet it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.”
He told them still another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.”
Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables. He did not tell them anything without using a parable.
So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.”
Then Jesus dismissed the crowds and went into the house. His disciples came to Him and said, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.”
He replied, “The One who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.
The field is the world, and the good seed represents the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one,
and the enemy who sows them is the devil. The harvest is the {{synteleia|end of the age}}, and the harvesters are angels.
As the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age.
The Son of Man will send out His angels, and they will weed out of His kingdom every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness.
And they will throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.

units.label: Treasure, pearl, and net
units.note: worth everything, and a final sorting

verses.text: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. When a man found it, he hid it again, and in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls.
When he found one very precious pearl, he went away and sold all he had and bought it.
Once again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was cast into the sea and caught all kinds of fish.
When it was full, the men pulled it ashore. Then they sat down and sorted the good fish into containers, but threw the bad away.
So will it be at the end of the age: The angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous
and throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Have you understood all these things?” “Yes,” they answered.
Then He told them, “For this reason, every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.”
When Jesus had finished these parables, He withdrew from that place.

parabole.gloss: Parable, a comparison or story laid alongside a truth to illustrate it. Jesus' parables both reveal the kingdom to those who receive them and veil it from the hardened, so that the same story enlightens the humble and hides truth from the proud.

mysterion.gloss: Mystery, a secret now disclosed. The mysteries of the kingdom are the once-hidden ways God's reign actually comes, granted to the disciples but withheld from those who will not receive; not puzzles to solve but revelation to be given.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, reign, royal rule. The parables repeatedly begin the kingdom of heaven is like, unveiling its present, hidden, growing, and mixed character before its glorious consummation at the end of the age.

synteleia.gloss: The end, or consummation, of the age. The harvest of the parables is this final moment when the Son of Man sends His angels to separate the wicked from the righteous, ending the present overlap of good and evil.

basic.context: After rising rejection, Jesus sits in a boat and teaches the crowds in parables. He tells of a sower whose seed lands on four kinds of soil, of wheat and weeds growing together, of a tiny mustard seed and hidden leaven, of treasure and a priceless pearl, and of a net that catches all kinds of fish. To His disciples He explains that these stories unveil the secrets of the kingdom, while veiling them from hardened hearts.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the parables as a set, each opening a facet of how the kingdom comes. It arrives now, but hidden and small; it meets varied responses; it grows secretly; it lets good and evil coexist until the harvest; it is worth everything; and it ends in judgment. Notice that Jesus explains two parables, giving us the key to reading the rest, and that parables both reveal and conceal by design.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus teaches in parables, stories laid alongside the truth. He gives the disciples the mysteries of the kingdom, secrets now disclosed to those who receive. The kingdom of heaven is His constant subject, and its climax is the end of the age, when the Son of Man will send His angels to separate the wicked from the righteous.
basic.typology: The sower and the harvest draw on the prophets' images of God planting and reaping His people. The mustard tree in which birds nest echoes Old Testament pictures of a kingdom sheltering the nations. And the final separation, the furnace and the shining righteous, fulfills Daniel's vision of the wise shining like the stars.
basic.christ: Jesus is the sower who scatters the word of the kingdom, and He is the Son of Man who will send His angels at the harvest to gather and to judge. He is the treasure and the pearl worth selling everything to gain. And He is the one who reveals the mysteries hidden since the foundation of the world.
basic.god: God's kingdom comes on His terms: not in overwhelming display but quietly, patiently, and irresistibly. He is patient with the mixed field, not uprooting evil prematurely, yet He will surely judge at the end. He grants understanding to the humble and gives more to those who receive, while the hardened lose even what they have.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 6:9-10 is quoted about hearing but not understanding. Psalm 78:2 is the prophecy of speaking in parables. Daniel 12:3 lies behind the righteous shining like the sun. And Ezekiel 17 pictures a tree sheltering the birds, like the mustard seed.
basic.oneStory: Rejected by many, Jesus reveals that the kingdom has come in a way no one expected: hidden in a word, small as a seed, mixed with evil, growing secretly toward a certain harvest. It is worth everything to gain, and it will end in a great separation. The story of God's reign is unfolding now, quietly and surely, until the Son of Man gathers His own and the righteous shine like the sun.

context.literary:
Matthew 13 is the third of the five great discourses of the Gospel, and it is the only one made almost entirely of stories. It also has a clear two-part shape. Verses 1 to 35 are spoken from a boat to the crowds on the shore: the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed and the leaven. At verse 36 Jesus dismisses the crowds and goes into the house, and the rest, verses 36 to 52, is for the disciples alone: the weeds explained, then the treasure, the pearl and the net. That makes seven parables in all, four in public and three in private, and the closing saying about the scribe, verse 52, adds an eighth picture that turns the lesson on the hearer.

The movement of the chapter is from sowing to harvest. The first parable asks what happens to the word when it is sown; the weeds and the net carry the story to the end of the age; the mustard seed and the leaven describe what the kingdom looks like in between. The explanations are placed with care. The sower is explained at once, verses 18 to 23, and the weeds at the house, verses 36 to 43, so that the first and the longest parables are interpreted for us, while the others are left to be understood by comparison.

There are echoes within the chapter that reward notice. 'He who has ears, let him hear' closes the sower, verse 9, and the weeds, verse 43, so that the first explanation and the last begin and end with the same summons. The phrase 'the end of the age' and the furnace with its weeping and gnashing of teeth appear in both the weeds and the net, verses 40 to 42 and 49 to 50. The treasure and the pearl form a pair in the same way as the mustard seed and the leaven, a man and a woman, a field and a kitchen, as Luke often pairs them.

The chapter also sits within a sequence of rejection. It begins 'that same day,' referring to the day in chapter 12 when the Pharisees called Jesus' power satanic and He redefined His family, and it ends with the rejection at Nazareth in verses 53 to 58. The parables thus explain why the kingdom is received by some and not by others.
context.historical:
The boat was a natural pulpit. The Sea of Galilee has a shoreline that slopes gently upward from the water, and a speaker in a boat a short distance out can be heard by a large crowd on the shore, which is what verse 2 describes. Many of the hearers worked the land or the lake, so the stories were about what they did every day.

The scene of the sower would have been familiar. In the farming of the region, seed was commonly broadcast by hand across the field and then ploughed in, so the path, rocks and thorns were all part of the same field, not separate plots. Footpaths ran along and through fields, the limestone bedrock lay close beneath a thin layer of soil in many places, and thorns were perennial weeds whose roots survived the winter. A yield of a hundredfold was extraordinary; the best known Old Testament instance is Genesis 26:12, where it is a sign of the LORD's blessing on Isaac. The picture is not one of an ordinary good year but of an abundance that no farmer could produce by his own efforts.

The weeds of verse 25 are most likely darnel, a grass whose seedlings look very like wheat until the ears form, which is why the owner will not risk uprooting the wheat with it. The enemy's deed was an act of spite, one of a kind that could happen in a rural community.

Mustard grows from a very small seed into a shrub that can stand taller than a man, and 'smallest of all seeds' is the language of the proverb, not a botanical claim. Three measures of flour, the three seahs of Genesis 18:6, is a large amount, enough to feed a great household. The treasure hidden in a field reflects a world where valuables were often buried for safekeeping, and a man who found someone else's buried wealth could secure it only by buying the land. Pearls were among the most expensive of ornaments. The dragnet of verse 47 was hauled onto the beach and its catch sorted by hand; the Law of Moses already divided sea creatures into those fit to eat and those not, Leviticus 11:9 to 12.

The 'scribe' of verse 52 was the trained teacher of the Law. Matthew may well have seen his own task, as a Gospel writer steeped in the Scriptures, in this description.
context.canonical:
The parables are rooted in the Old Testament throughout. The quotation in verses 14 and 15 is Isaiah 6:9 to 10, from the prophet's commission, and it is quoted again in John 12:39 to 40 and Acts 28:25 to 27, so that all the Gospels and Acts return to the same text to explain the nation's response. The quotation in verse 35 is Psalm 78:2, in which Asaph says, 'I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning.' Matthew's 'from the foundation of the world' widens the Psalm's reach, and he presents Asaph's words as a prophecy fulfilled in Jesus.

The imagery of God as sower is found in Jeremiah 31:27 and Hosea 2:23, where the LORD sows His people in the land. The tree that shelters the birds echoes Ezekiel 17:22 to 23, where God plants a shoot on the mountain heights of Israel and birds of every kind nest under it, and the great trees of Ezekiel 31:6 and Daniel 4:12, where the birds and beasts shelter beneath a world power. The righteous who shine like the sun reflect Daniel 12:3, and the harvest and sickle recall Joel 3:13, taken up in Revelation 14:15 to 16.

The New Testament carries the themes forward. Mark 4:26 to 29 gives the parable of the seed that grows by itself, and Luke 8:11 says plainly, 'The seed is the word of God.' Luke 13:18 to 21 repeats the mustard seed and the leaven. Paul calls the gospel a mystery 'hidden for ages' that is now revealed, Colossians 1:26 and Romans 16:25 to 26, which is exactly what Jesus says here. Peter says that believers are born again of imperishable seed, 1 Peter 1:23. The Lord's patience toward the world in the weeds is explained in 2 Peter 3:9, and the separation at the end is described in Matthew 25:31 to 33.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew arranges this chapter to explain a puzzle that troubled the first Christians: if the Messiah has come, why is the kingdom so small, so mixed and so widely refused? The parables answer that this is exactly how the kingdom was meant to arrive. It comes as a word, scattered widely and received in different ways. It grows quietly, like seed, and does not take over by force. It is accompanied by an enemy who sows his own crop. And it will be vindicated at a harvest which is certain and in God's hands. Matthew wants his readers to hear in that a call to patience and to trust.

He also wants to explain the strange rhythm of Jesus' ministry, in which the same words enlighten some and leave others untouched. Jesus' use of Isaiah 6 does not say that He wants people to miss the truth, but that the hardening already at work in the nation is being met by a form of speech that requires a hearing heart. The listener who comes close and asks, as the disciples do, receives explanation; the one who stays at a distance receives only the story.

And the chapter is meant to produce a particular kind of disciple. The last saying, verse 52, tells every learner of the kingdom to become a householder who brings out both new and old treasures, someone who understands what Jesus has said and shares it, while keeping faith with the Scriptures of Israel. The point is not to be amused by stories but to understand, and to act on understanding by selling all for the kingdom and bearing fruit.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These parables describe how the kingdom works, and Jesus' own explanations show that they are meant to be applied. The sower does not tell the hearer to be a certain soil; it invites self-examination, asking what is choking, shallow or hard in a person, and what kind of hearing produces fruit. The fact that the explanations are given by Jesus Himself, in verses 18 to 23 and 36 to 43, gives a sound guide for interpretation: a parable has a central point, and the details are to be read in its light.

Not every feature of a parable is a teaching or a model. The man in verse 44 hides the treasure again before buying the field; Jesus does not hold this up as an example of business ethics, but uses it to show the joy that drives the sale. The farmer who allows the weeds to grow describes God's patience; it does not forbid church discipline, which the same Gospel prescribes in Matthew 18:15 to 17 and which the apostles practised, 1 Corinthians 5:1 to 5. The field is 'the world,' verse 38, so the parable speaks first of the final judgment and not of a method of governing the church.

The harsh statement about the hardened is a description of a pattern, not a command to leave anyone unaddressed. Believers are told to sow the word everywhere, as the sower does, and to leave the result and the sorting to God. Finally, the numbers, a hundredfold, sixty and thirty, are not a quota but a picture of real fruit. The text expects some fruit from every genuine hearer, though not the same amount.

debates.question: Why does Jesus teach in parables that both reveal and conceal?

views.label: A gracious revelation to the receptive
views.case: To the disciples, parables open the mysteries of the kingdom; those with a humble, hearing heart are given more, so the parables are a gift of understanding to those who receive Jesus.

views.label: A judicial hiding from the hardened
views.case: Quoting Isaiah 6, Jesus shows that parables also veil the truth from those who have closed their eyes, a righteous response to persistent rejection that leaves them ever hearing but never understanding.

debates.bearing: Both are true at once: the same parable enlightens the humble and hides truth from the proud, so that the form of Jesus' teaching itself sifts hearts.

debates.question: Why are the weeds left to grow among the wheat until the harvest?

views.label: God's patience delays judgment
views.case: Pulling the weeds early would harm the wheat; God withholds final judgment to give time and to protect His people, tolerating the present mixture of good and evil in the world.

views.label: Judgment is certain but reserved for the end
views.case: The delay is not indifference; the harvest will surely come, when the Son of Man's angels separate and judge, so the present coexistence is temporary, not permanent.

debates.bearing: Both hold that believers must live faithfully amid a mixed world, neither presuming to enact final judgment now nor doubting that God will justly judge at the end of the age.

debates.question: Is the field of the wheat and weeds the church or the world?

views.label: The field is the world, as Jesus says
views.case: Verse 38 states that the field is the world, and the parable ends with the Son of Man's angels gathering out of His kingdom all causes of sin. The sowing is done everywhere, and the mixture is of all people. This is the plain reading and the one held by most of the Reformers.

views.label: The field includes the visible church
views.case: Augustine used the parable against those who wished to purge the church of every impure member, and many readers have applied it to the mixed membership of congregations. The weeds were sown among the wheat, and the 'sons of the kingdom' and 'sons of the evil one' live side by side.

debates.bearing: The text identifies the field as the world, so the parable is primarily about the world until the end. Yet the lesson of patience applies within the church, where a weed cannot be reliably told from wheat by human sight, even though other passages call for discipline of open and unrepentant sin.

debates.question: Is the leaven an image of good or of evil?

views.label: It pictures the kingdom's pervasive growth
views.case: The parable begins 'the kingdom of heaven is like leaven,' and the point of comparison is the effect: a small amount that works through the whole batch. Luke 13:21 gives the same saying with the same positive purpose, and the woman is the one doing the right thing.

views.label: It pictures the corrupting presence of evil in the kingdom
views.case: Leaven elsewhere is a sign of corruption, Matthew 16:6 to 12 and 1 Corinthians 5:6 to 8, and the woman 'hid' it, so some read the parable as warning that the kingdom's outward form will be infiltrated. This view was common among certain interpreters of the last two centuries.

debates.bearing: The weight of the context favours growth. Jesus pairs the leaven with the mustard seed, and a parable can use a familiar image in a new way. The difference between these views is real but not final: both agree that the kingdom's progress is hidden and that the end will be a full harvest.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for these stories, parabole, is built from a verb meaning to throw or place alongside, so a parable sets one thing next to another for comparison. In the Greek Old Testament it commonly renders the Hebrew mashal, a word that covers proverbs, riddles, taunts and wise sayings, which is why Matthew can quote Psalm 78:2 as a prophecy about parables. A parable is therefore not a children's tale but a riddle that calls for thought, and Jesus' 'Have you understood all these things?' in verse 51 expects an answer.

The disciples are given 'the mysteries of the kingdom.' The Greek word is mysterion, and in the Greek of Daniel 2:28 it describes what God alone reveals to the wise. In the New Testament a mystery is not something eternally unknowable but a secret that God has kept and now discloses, Colossians 1:26. It is plural here, since the parables unfold several truths, where Mark has the singular.

Understanding is the thread that runs through the sower. The verb synienai, to understand or grasp, occurs of the one on the path, 'does not understand it,' verse 19, and of the good soil, 'hears the word and understands it,' verse 23. The difference between the failures and the success is not simply the reception of the word but the grasp of it. Matthew's quotation from Isaiah, 'ever hearing but never understanding,' uses the same verb in verses 13 and 14.

The quotation in verse 14 reproduces the Hebrew idiom of the Greek translation of Isaiah 6:9, 'hearing you will hear,' an emphatic doubling that Matthew keeps. The verb for 'grown callous' in verse 15 means to become thick or fat, which is the picture of a heart so dulled that it no longer responds.

In the sower's explanation, the shallow hearer 'at once' receives the word with joy, and when persecution comes he 'quickly' falls away. Both adverbs are the same Greek word, euthys, and the verb for 'falls away' is skandalizo, literally to be tripped up, the verb from which we get scandal. The quick joy and quick collapse are two sides of the same shallowness.

The verb in verse 41, 'weed out,' is literally to collect, and its objects are 'every cause of sin,' skandala, the things that trip others up, and 'all who practice lawlessness,' anomia. Anomia is a key word in Matthew, where Jesus uses it of those who say 'Lord, Lord' and are rejected, Matthew 7:23, and predicts its increase, Matthew 24:12.

In verse 52 the scribe 'has been discipled,' using the verb mathēteuo. It is the same verb that appears in the Great Commission, Matthew 28:19, 'make disciples.' The hearer who understands has become a learner in the kingdom, and a learner who is also a teacher.

typology.type: The sower and the sown people, Matthew 13:3
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament speaks of the LORD sowing His people. Jeremiah 31:27 promises that He will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and Hosea 2:23 says, 'I will sow her as My own in the land.' Jesus takes up the figure and makes it more personal, the Son of Man as the sower, and the seed is the word, the sons of the kingdom and the message together. The escalation is that sowing now reaches all nations, since the field is the world. It also deepens the cost: in John 12:24 the seed is Jesus Himself, who must fall into the ground and die before there is much fruit. The picture is not complete until the harvest.

typology.type: The tree that shelters the birds, Matthew 13:32
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel 17:22 to 23 promises that God will plant a tender shoot on Israel's high mountain, and it will become a majestic cedar under which birds of every kind find shelter. Ezekiel 31 and Daniel 4 use the same image of a world empire in whose branches the nations rest. Jesus applies the picture to the kingdom, which begins smaller than a seed and becomes a place of shelter for all peoples. The correspondence is real, since Gentiles are gathered under the kingdom's shade. But the empire trees of Ezekiel and Daniel are cut down in pride; this tree is planted by God and never felled.

Israel was God's 'treasured possession,' segullah, Exodus 19:5, and Psalm 135:4 says that the LORD chose Jacob as His own treasured possession. Malachi 3:17 uses it of those who feared the LORD and will be His 'on the day when I prepare My treasured possession.' The parable of the treasure in the field can be read against that background as the picture of a man who finds something so valuable that he sacrifices everything to have it. The correspondence runs in two directions, as the believer treasures the kingdom and, as Ephesians 1:14 and Titus 2:14 suggest, God treasures His people, bought at a price. The picture falls short because the parable has no place for grace; the man pays, whereas the gospel says the price was paid for us.

typology.type: The great harvest and the separation, Matthew 13:39 to 43
typology.fulfillment: The prophets saw the end as a harvest and a refining. Joel 3:13 calls for the sickle because the harvest is ripe, Malachi 3:18 says that the LORD's people will again distinguish between the righteous and the wicked, and Daniel 12:3 says that the wise will shine like the heavens. Jesus fills in the picture: the harvesters are angels, the sower is the Son of Man, and the righteous will shine like the sun in the Father's kingdom. Revelation 14:15 to 16 shows the sickle swung, and Matthew 25:31 to 33 shows the great sorting. The type is fulfilled in part, since the Son of Man has come, and in part still to come, since the harvest is future.

typology.type: The householder with new and old treasure, Matthew 13:52
typology.fulfillment: Ezra was 'a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses,' Ezra 7:6, and the scribes of Jesus' day preserved and applied the old Scriptures. Jesus' scribe is one who has been discipled in the kingdom, and so brings out of the storeroom things both new and old. The treasure of the Old Testament is not discarded but shown in its true light, as the Sermon on the Mount says that the Law and the Prophets are fulfilled, Matthew 5:17. In Matthew 23:34 Jesus sends 'prophets and wise men and teachers,' and the church's teachers continue the pattern. The correspondence breaks down only if the new is made to replace the old; Jesus keeps both.

study.christ:
Jesus is the sower. The first parable pictures one who goes out to sow, and the explanation of the weeds says plainly, 'The One who sows the good seed is the Son of Man,' verse 37. The title is from Daniel 7:13 to 14, where one like a son of man receives dominion and a kingdom that will never be destroyed, so that the humble sower of Galilee is also the king who will be given every nation. That is the double identity that the parables hold together: the Son of Man sows in apparent weakness and reaps in glory.

He is also the one who reveals what was hidden. Asaph's Psalm said, 'I will utter things hidden from the beginning,' and Matthew presents Jesus as the one in whose mouth that promise is kept. In Matthew 11:25 to 27 He thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children, and says that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him. The mysteries of the kingdom are not an abstract body of information but are known through Him. Paul sums it up in Colossians 1:27 as 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.'

He is the treasure and the pearl, though the parables leave the identification unstated. The kingdom is worth everything because the King has come. Paul counts all things loss 'compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord,' Philippians 3:8, which is the response of the finder in verses 44 and 46. Yet it must not be forgotten that He is also the one who pays. The man who buys the field acts like Christ, who gave Himself to redeem a people, so that the parables of the treasure can be read both ways without contradiction.

He is the seed that dies. In John 12:24 Jesus says that unless a kernel of wheat falls into the ground and dies it remains a seed, but if it dies it bears much fruit. The mustard seed's smallness and the buried seed's death point to the same shape of His work: the kingdom grows out of an apparent defeat. And He is the Son of Man who will send His angels, verse 41. The same Jesus who sits in a boat speaking to a crowd will be seated on His glorious throne, Matthew 25:31, and will separate the sheep from the goats.

A caution is in order. Jesus explains only two of these parables, and in both the explanation matches each detail to a person or event. It would be a mistake to treat every detail in the other parables, such as the three measures or the number of fish, as a code. The christological links here rest on Jesus' own explanations and on the New Testament's use of these images, and not on invented allegory.
study.god:
The parables show God as one who works by seed and not by force. His kingdom comes through a word that is scattered with a generous hand and that grows with a life of its own. Mark's version of the seed growing secretly says that the earth produces a crop 'all by itself,' Mark 4:28, and Isaiah 55:10 to 11 says that God's word does not return empty but accomplishes what He pleases. The power is in the seed, which is to say in God. This takes away from the preacher both despair and pride: the sower sows, and the harvest is the Lord's.

God is patient. The owner of the field does not allow the servants to pull up the weeds, because he cares for the wheat. In the end this is the patience of 2 Peter 3:9, which says that the Lord is 'not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.' But it is not weak. The harvest is as certain as the sowing, and the Son of Man's angels will gather and burn. Nothing in the parables suggests that God is unaware of evil or unable to deal with it. The enemy is an enemy, his work is recognised for what it is, and the verdict is already settled.

God is the one who reveals. The mysteries are given to the disciples, verse 11, and the Father's good pleasure is the cause, Matthew 11:26. This is not an arbitrary favouritism, since the parable of the sower insists that people hear and respond for real reasons, and Jesus' language of hardening has the nation's own persistent unbelief in view. But it teaches that understanding is a gift. A person who sees the kingdom should thank God and not congratulate himself.

God is generous. He plants seed that yields a hundredfold, and He makes the kingdom a shelter for the nations. And he is holy: the furnace and the weeping and gnashing of teeth, verses 42 and 50, are not decorations, and the same Jesus who tells of the treasure tells of the fire. The two belong together because the kingdom is worth everything, and so to lose it is the greatest loss.

For worship, the passage invites at least three responses. One is a hearing that gets down to understanding, since the cry 'He who has ears, let him hear' is repeated. Another is joy, the sort that leads a man to sell all he has. And the last is patient hope, the willingness to live in the mixed field without either despairing or taking judgment into our own hands, trusting the God who will bring in His harvest in His own time.

crossReferences.note: The prophet is commissioned to preach to a people whose hearts have grown dull. Jesus applies this to the response to His own teaching, as do John 12:39 to 40 and Acts 28:25 to 27. The passage's concluding hope, that they might turn and be healed, shows that the hardening is a judgment with a purpose, not a final word.

Asaph's promise to open his mouth in parables and speak of things hidden from the beginning is the text Matthew says is fulfilled. The Psalm goes on to recount Israel's history, which shows the parables to be no isolated device but part of a long tradition of teaching through story.

Isaac sowed in the land and reaped a hundredfold that year, and the text says the LORD blessed him. This is the Old Testament's picture of an extraordinary harvest, and it frames the hundredfold of the good soil as the product of God's blessing and not of ordinary farming.

God plants a shoot on the mountain heights of Israel that grows into a majestic cedar, with birds of every kind nesting in its shade. The tree of the mustard seed echoes it, and the birds suggest the nations coming to shelter under the kingdom that begins small.

Nebuchadnezzar's great tree, with beasts in its shade and the birds of the air nesting in its branches, is explained as an earthly kingdom. Jesus reuses the image for a different kingdom, one that begins smaller than the smallest seed and is never cut down.

The wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars. This stands behind the saying that the righteous will shine like the sun in the Father's kingdom, which makes the end of the weeds parable a promise of glory.

The call to swing the sickle because the harvest is ripe pairs harvest with the judgment of the nations. The same imagery of the sickle returns in Revelation 14:15 to 16, so that the harvesters of the parable stand in a long line of prophetic pictures of the end.

Mark alone records the parable of the seed that grows secretly, in which the sower sleeps and wakes and the earth produces a crop by itself. It complements Matthew's emphasis on the hidden growth of the kingdom, and the sickle at the end gives the same promise of harvest.

Luke's explanation of the sower begins with the simplest possible gloss, 'The seed is the word of God.' It confirms that the parable is about the hearing of the message of the kingdom, and it guards the reader from treating the soils as fixed types of person.

A little earlier, Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children. It explains the dynamic of verses 10 to 17, where the disciples are given understanding that the crowds lack, and rests it on the Father's good pleasure.

Paul describes the mystery hidden for ages and generations now revealed to the saints, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. It shows how the apostles understood the 'mysteries of the kingdom' that Jesus gave His disciples and extended them to the Gentiles.

The Son of Man comes in glory with all the angels and separates the nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. It confirms that the sorting of the weeds and the net is the work of the returning Christ and that the harvest of Matthew 13 and the judgment of Matthew 25 are the same event.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden and with seed. In Genesis 1 God commands the earth to produce seed-bearing plants, and the first promise of rescue is made to the woman's 'seed,' Genesis 3:15. From then on the story is full of sowing and harvest, of famine and fruit, of a people planted in a land and uprooted from it, and of a God who promises to sow them again, Jeremiah 31:27 and Hosea 2:23. The parables of Matthew 13 take up that long story at a turning point. The sower has come, and the seed is the word of the kingdom.

They also answer questions the whole Old Testament leaves open. Why did Israel hear so often and understand so little? Isaiah 6 said that it was part of the prophet's calling to meet that hardness, and Jesus shows that the same pattern continues in His own ministry. Why does evil continue to grow among the good? The enemy of Genesis 3 is still sowing, and the parable of the weeds shows that his work is allowed for a time and will be dealt with at the end. Why is the kingdom not more obviously glorious? Because it grows from small things, as it always has, from the seed of Abraham and the shoot from the stump of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1.

The parables set up the rest of Matthew. After them come the rejection at Nazareth, the death of John, and the movement to the cross, where the seed falls into the ground and dies, John 12:24. They also set up the commission of Matthew 28, where the Lord who has all authority sends His disciples to sow among all nations and promises to be with them to the end of the age, Matthew 28:20. The scribe of verse 52 is the first sketch of the apostolic teacher.

The story ends in a harvest. Revelation 14 shows the sickle swung, and the sorting of the net and the weeds is completed. Daniel's wise shine, and the righteous shine like the sun in the Father's kingdom. The tree of life stands in the city, and the nations bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:24 and 22:2. The little seed has become the shelter of the world, the treasure is possessed, and the one who sowed with tears reaps with shouts of joy, Psalm 126:5 to 6.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the sower teach about responses to the word?

options.text: The same word meets different hearts, and only the good soil hears, understands, and bears fruit.
options.note: Verses 18-23 explain the four soils and the fruitful heart.

options.text: The word will always fail unless the sower works harder.
options.note: The sower sows the same seed; the difference is the soil, the heart's response, not the sower's effort.

options.text: Everyone who hears the word will eventually bear fruit.
options.note: Three of the four soils do not bear lasting fruit; response varies decisively.

options.text: Only those who never face trouble can be saved.
options.note: The good soil bears fruit even amid a world of trouble; trials expose shallow soil rather than defining the saved.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus teach in parables?

options.text: They reveal the kingdom's mysteries to the receptive and veil them from the hardened.
options.note: Verses 11-15 show parables both granting understanding and fulfilling Isaiah's hardening.

options.text: Only to make His teaching easier for everyone to grasp.
options.note: They do illustrate truth, but Jesus says they also conceal it from hardened hearts, which this misses.

options.text: To entertain the crowds without any real meaning.
options.note: The parables carry weighty meaning about the kingdom, not mere entertainment.

options.text: Because He did not want anyone to understand Him.
options.note: He gives the mysteries to the disciples; the concealing is a judgment on the hardened, not a blanket refusal to be understood.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the wheat and the weeds teach?

options.text: Good and evil grow together until the harvest, when the Son of Man will separate and judge.
options.note: Verses 24-30 and 36-43 show the delayed but certain final separation.

options.text: Believers should root out all evildoers from the world now.
options.note: The owner forbids pulling the weeds early; judgment is reserved for the harvest, not enacted by us now.

options.text: The weeds and wheat are actually the same in the end.
options.note: They are decisively separated at the harvest, not treated as the same.

options.text: God is indifferent to the presence of evil.
options.note: The delay is patience, not indifference; judgment is certain at the end of the age.

quiz.q: What do the mustard seed and the leaven reveal about the kingdom?

options.text: It begins small and hidden yet grows and spreads until its effect is vast.
options.note: Verses 31-33 picture the kingdom's secret, pervasive growth from tiny beginnings.

options.text: The kingdom will always remain small and insignificant.
options.note: The opposite; from small beginnings it grows large and permeates the whole, so this misses the growth.

options.text: The kingdom comes only through sudden, visible power.
options.note: These parables stress hidden, gradual growth, not sudden display.

options.text: The kingdom depends entirely on human effort to expand.
options.note: The seed grows and the leaven works by their own hidden power, picturing God's work, not mere human effort.

quiz.q: What do the treasure and the pearl teach about the kingdom's worth?

options.text: It is worth joyfully selling all one has to gain.
options.note: Verses 44-46 show both men gladly giving everything for the surpassing treasure.

options.text: It can be obtained cheaply and without any cost.
options.note: The kingdom is a free gift, yet these parables stress it is worth surrendering everything, which this denies.

options.text: It is valuable only to the wealthy who can afford it.
options.note: The value is the kingdom itself; the point is glad, total commitment, not personal wealth.

options.text: It is one good thing among many equally worthy pursuits.
options.note: The parables present it as supremely valuable, worth more than everything else combined.

questions: The same seed fell on four soils with very different results. What kind of soil is your heart right now, and what would it take to become good soil that bears lasting fruit?
The kingdom often comes hidden and small, like a seed or leaven, rather than in overwhelming display. Where are you tempted to despise God's quiet, gradual work and demand something more dramatic?
Jesus said the wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest. How does trusting God's timing for final judgment free you from bitterness while you live faithfully in a mixed world?
The man sold everything with joy to gain the treasure. What would it look like for you to treasure the kingdom above all your other pursuits and possessions?
There is a real end of the age and a real separation. How does the certainty of final judgment sober you and move you to make sure your own heart is good soil?

translationNotes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 6:9-10, describing a people who hear and see but do not understand, applied to those hardened against Jesus.
I will open My mouth in parables quotes Psalm 78:2; Matthew presents Jesus' parabolic teaching as a fulfillment of Scripture.
